candidate.answerReason: The prime product of the positive integer roots forces them to be 1 and q. Their prime sum q+1 then forces q=2 and p=3, making all four statements true.

methods.label: Use the sum and product of the roots
methods.explanation:
Let the distinct positive integer roots be \(u\) and \(v\). Expanding their monic quadratic shows how the coefficients encode their sum and product:
\[
(x-u)(x-v)=x^2-(u+v)x+uv.
\]
Comparing with \(x^2-px+q\) gives
\[
u+v=p,\qquad uv=q.
\]
Since \(q\) is prime, its only positive integer factor pair is \(1,q\). Thus the roots are \(1\) and \(q\), and \(p=q+1\).

Now \(q\ge2\), so \(p\ge3\). A prime at least \(3\) is odd, making \(q=p-1\) even. The only even prime is \(2\), so necessarily \(q=2\) and \(p=3\). These values give the distinct positive roots \(1\) and \(2\), so they satisfy the original conditions.

The difference of the roots is \(1\), which is odd; the root \(2\) is prime; \(p^2-q=9-2=7\) is prime; and \(p+q=3+2=5\) is prime. All four statements are true, choice E.
